Pipeline runs
Per-step status and logs for each DAG
2 · Grafana
Cluster & GPU
Nodes, Kueue queues, DCGM GPU metrics

panels.title: MLflow runs (all time)
panels.description: Counts every active run in the MLflow backend database, ignoring the dashboard time range — unlike the chart panels, which are filtered. Retitled so the number is not read as runs within the selected window.

targets.rawSql: SELECT count(*) AS "runs" FROM runs r JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id WHERE r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active';

panels.title: Latest gate decision
panels.description: The most recent gate decision, so the dashboard answers 'is the current checkpoint shippable' without scrolling. PASS is not PROMOTE: open-loop MSE can clear a ceiling but cannot certify task success.

targets.rawSql: SELECT coalesce(dec.value, 'none') AS "decision" FROM runs r JOIN params mt ON mt.run_uuid = r.run_uuid AND mt.key = 'gate_metric' LEFT JOIN params dec ON dec.run_uuid = r.run_uuid AND dec.key = 'gate_decision' WHERE r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' ORDER BY r.start_time DESC LIMIT 1;

panels.title: Recent MLflow runs
panels.description: The 10 most recently started runs, straight from the MLflow backend database.

targets.rawSql: SELECT to_timestamp(r.start_time / 1000) AS "started", e.name AS "experiment", r.name AS "run", r.status AS "status", round((coalesce(r.end_time, (extract(epoch from now()) * 1000)::bigint) - r.start_time) / 60000.0, 1) AS "minutes", (SELECT count(DISTINCT m.key) FROM metrics m WHERE m.run_uuid = r.run_uuid) AS "metrics" FROM runs r JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id WHERE r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active' ORDER BY r.start_time DESC LIMIT 10;

panels.title: MLflow — mean reward by run
panels.description: Isaac Lab's reward scalar arrives as 'Train/mean_reward' with the slash intact: the sanitizer in examples/rl/mlflow_isaaclab.py permits '/', so it does not become 'Train_mean_reward'. The underscored key is matched as well because older runs carry it. The time filter uses $__unixEpochFilter because metrics.timestamp is epoch milliseconds, and because $__timeFilter() truncates its argument at the first ')' — a nested to_timestamp() call would compare a bigint against an RFC 3339 string.

targets.rawSql: SELECT to_timestamp(m.timestamp / 1000) AS "time", r.name AS metric, m.value FROM metrics m JOIN runs r ON r.run_uuid = m.run_uuid JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id WHERE m.key IN ('Train/mean_reward', 'Train_mean_reward', 'rollout_ep_rew_mean') AND r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND $__unixEpochFilter(m.timestamp / 1000) ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: GR00T fine-tune — training loss
panels.description: HF Trainer logs 'loss' per logging_steps; the RL reward panel above never matches a fine-tune because the GR00T run reports Trainer keys instead. Matching the experiment on 'vla-finetune%' keeps the legacy experiment (vla-finetune-legacy, kept because MLflow cannot move an experiment's artifact_location) in the same panel.

targets.rawSql: SELECT to_timestamp(m.timestamp / 1000) AS "time", r.name AS metric, m.value FROM metrics m JOIN runs r ON r.run_uuid = m.run_uuid JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id WHERE m.key = 'loss' AND e.name LIKE 'vla-finetune%' AND r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND $__unixEpochFilter(m.timestamp / 1000) ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: GR00T fine-tune — learning rate and grad norm
panels.description: Two keys on one panel on purpose: a loss that stops moving is read together with whether the schedule is still stepping and whether gradients are exploding. Log scale because the two differ by orders of magnitude.

targets.rawSql: SELECT to_timestamp(m.timestamp / 1000) AS "time", r.name || ' · ' || m.key AS metric, m.value FROM metrics m JOIN runs r ON r.run_uuid = m.run_uuid JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id WHERE m.key IN ('learning_rate', 'grad_norm') AND e.name LIKE 'vla-finetune%' AND r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND $__unixEpochFilter(m.timestamp / 1000) ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: GPU utilization per node (DCGM)
panels.description: Empty while the GPU instance group is scaled to 0.

panels.title: Gate decisions — promote / pass / block
panels.description: Every decision examples/vla/gate_checkpoint.py has made, newest first. This is the row that closes the development loop: the eval panels below say how a checkpoint scored, this one says whether that score was allowed to matter. BLOCK means the gate Job exited non-zero, so the Argo workflow failed and anything chained behind it never ran. The reasons column is the only durable copy of why - the Job log is deleted by ttlSecondsAfterFinished. Two metrics with different powers: openloop_mse is behaviour-cloning fidelity and can only block, so a clean run reads PASS, not PROMOTE; success_rate comes from real-robot or closed-loop trials and can promote, filling in the alias column. Only one of episodes / trials is filled per row, and which one tells you what kind of evidence the decision rests on: episodes counts recorded trajectories replayed open-loop, trials counts attempts at the actual task. They are not interchangeable sample counts, so they get separate columns rather than one n. Read whichever is filled before trusting the value - 3 episodes and 24 trials carry very different weight, and the threshold is applied to the mean either way.

targets.rawSql: SELECT to_timestamp(r.start_time / 1000) AS "decided", coalesce(dec.value, '?') AS "decision", regexp_replace(coalesce(ckpt.value, r.name), '^.*/', '') AS "checkpoint", mt.value AS "metric", round(coalesce(mse.value, sr.value)::numeric, 3) AS "value", thr.value AS "limit", ep.value::int AS "episodes", tr.value::int AS "trials", coalesce(prom.value, '') AS "alias", coalesce(why.value, '') AS "reasons" FROM runs r JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id LEFT JOIN params dec  ON dec.run_uuid  = r.run_uuid AND dec.key  = 'gate_decision' LEFT JOIN params ckpt ON ckpt.run_uuid = r.run_uuid AND ckpt.key = 'checkpoint' LEFT JOIN params mt   ON mt.run_uuid   = r.run_uuid AND mt.key   = 'gate_metric' LEFT JOIN params thr  ON thr.run_uuid  = r.run_uuid AND thr.key  = 'threshold' LEFT JOIN params prom ON prom.run_uuid = r.run_uuid AND prom.key = 'promoted_alias' LEFT JOIN params why  ON why.run_uuid  = r.run_uuid AND why.key  = 'gate_reasons' LEFT JOIN metrics mse ON mse.run_uuid  = r.run_uuid AND mse.key  = 'eval_openloop_mse' LEFT JOIN metrics sr  ON sr.run_uuid   = r.run_uuid AND sr.key   = 'eval_success_rate' LEFT JOIN metrics ep  ON ep.run_uuid   = r.run_uuid AND ep.key   = 'eval_episodes' LEFT JOIN metrics tr  ON tr.run_uuid   = r.run_uuid AND tr.key   = 'eval_total_trials' WHERE mt.value IS NOT NULL AND r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active' ORDER BY r.start_time DESC LIMIT 50;

panels.title: Open-loop eval — latest MSE per checkpoint
panels.description: One row per checkpoint, keeping only its most recent open-loop evaluation (DISTINCT ON). Answers 'which checkpoint on FSx is currently best'. MSE is behaviour-cloning fidelity against recorded trajectories, not task success rate — a low MSE does not imply the policy recovers out of distribution, so do not use it alone as a promotion gate. Populated by examples/vla/eval_closed_loop.py when MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI is set. episodes is how many trajectories the mean is over, and worst is the highest per-episode MSE. A mean under the gate ceiling with a worst far above it is one bad episode averaged away - the mean alone cannot show that.

targets.rawSql: SELECT DISTINCT ON (ckpt.value) regexp_replace(ckpt.value, '^.*/', '') AS "checkpoint", round(m.value::numeric, 3) AS "mse", round(mx.mx::numeric, 3) AS "worst", ep.value::int AS "episodes", to_timestamp(r.start_time / 1000) AS "evaluated" FROM metrics m JOIN runs r ON r.run_uuid = m.run_uuid JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id JOIN params ckpt ON ckpt.run_uuid = r.run_uuid AND ckpt.key = 'checkpoint' LEFT JOIN metrics ep ON ep.run_uuid = r.run_uuid AND ep.key = 'openloop_episodes' LEFT JOIN (SELECT run_uuid, max(value) AS mx FROM metrics            WHERE key = 'openloop_mse' GROUP BY run_uuid) mx       ON mx.run_uuid = r.run_uuid WHERE m.key = 'openloop_mse_mean' AND r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active' ORDER BY ckpt.value, r.start_time DESC;

panels.title: Open-loop MSE by eval run
panels.description: Mean MSE per evaluation run over time — shows whether more training actually lowers the error. Flattening between consecutive checkpoints is the signal to stop spending GPU hours. Uses $__unixEpochFilter because metrics.timestamp is epoch milliseconds, same as the mean-reward panel above.

targets.rawSql: SELECT to_timestamp(m.timestamp / 1000) AS "time", r.name AS metric, m.value FROM metrics m JOIN runs r ON r.run_uuid = m.run_uuid JOIN experiments e ON e.experiment_id = r.experiment_id WHERE m.key = 'openloop_mse_mean' AND r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND e.lifecycle_stage = 'active' AND $__unixEpochFilter(m.timestamp / 1000) ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Open-loop MSE per episode (latest eval)
panels.description: Per-episode breakdown of the most recent open-loop run; metrics.step holds the episode index. Surfaces failure modes the mean hides — a couple of bad episodes among otherwise good ones means the policy loses the trajectory under specific conditions. Follow up by replaying those recordings.

targets.rawSql: SELECT m.step AS "episode", m.value AS "mse" FROM metrics m WHERE m.key = 'openloop_mse' AND m.run_uuid = (SELECT r.run_uuid FROM runs r JOIN params p ON p.run_uuid = r.run_uuid AND p.key = 'eval_type' AND p.value = 'open_loop' WHERE r.lifecycle_stage = 'active' ORDER BY r.start_time DESC LIMIT 1) ORDER BY m.step;
